title: Financial Crises and the Short-Run Model

sections.title: Friction, deflation and the zero lower bound

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Welcome back. Today we are on financial crises and the short-run model: what happens to output and inflation when banks panic. Let's start with a weekend in late September 2008.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Ben Bernanke, head of the Fed, the central bank of the United States, met the leaders of Congress. He asked them to approve a huge rescue of the banks. Without it, he warned, there might be no economy by Monday.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the Fed cut interest rates, I suppose.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: It did. By the end of 2008, its rate was almost zero. Yet the slump was the worst since the Great Depression of the 1930s.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So here is today's question. Why did the 2008 crisis cause such a deep slump, even though the Fed cut its rate to zero?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: A slump, or recession, is a time when output and jobs fall. By the end of this episode, you'll be able to do three things. First, explain why extra interest for risk can hit spending like a fall in demand, and why a zero rate could not undo it. Second, explain how falling prices, with the interest rate stuck at zero, can turn a recession into a spiral. Third, describe the other tools the Fed and the government used, and what the data show about the slow recovery.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And we'll follow the chapter's mind map part by part?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. Part one is the crisis in the data. Part two builds the model: friction, deflation and the zero lower bound. Part three is policy and the aftermath. Each part has three to five leaves, small topics we take in order.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Part one of the map: The crisis in the data. The first leaf is the BAA spread. What's that?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: It's a credit rating, a grade for how safe a borrower is. BAA bonds are loans to solid companies that are not completely safe. The safe loan we compare them with is the U.S. government's 10-year bond, called a Treasury. The spread is the gap between their interest rates.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the spread is the extra interest a solid company pays, in case it doesn't repay.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Exactly. Economists call that extra interest a risk premium. From 1996 to 2007, the spread averaged 2.16 percentage points. A percentage point is the plain difference between two rates.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And in the crisis?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In December 2008, the spread reached 6.01 points, almost three times its usual size.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But the Fed was cutting its rate in 2008. So I'd guess companies paid less to borrow, too.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That's the natural guess, but it's wrong. From 2006 to 2008, the government's 10-year rate fell by more than a point, while the rate on BAA bonds went up by about a point. So the Fed's cuts reached the government, not the companies that build factories.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: the Fed rate. Remind me, which rate does the Fed set?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: The Fed is the Federal Reserve. It sets the fed funds rate, the rate banks charge one another for overnight loans. On Islandia, the imaginary island country of our examples, that's the policy rate of the Bank of Islandia, the island's central bank.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And after the crash?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: The fed funds rate was almost zero by the end of 2008, and it stayed there. From 2009 to 2015, it was never higher than 0.19 percent.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in the panic, money was very cheap for everyone.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: A lot of people think that, but not for firms. Firms pay the Fed's rate plus the risk premium. In late 2008, the premium had about tripled, so the rate on company bonds went up, not down.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: the price-earnings ratio. What does it measure?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company. Take an index of share prices, one number that follows many shares. Divide it by the average company profits of the past ten years, after inflation. Over the long run, that ratio has averaged about 18.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And before the great crashes?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In September 1929, just before the crash, the ratio reached 32.6, almost twice its long-run average. In December 1999, at the peak of the boom in internet shares, it reached 44.2, even higher. Both times, prices then fell a long way.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So those were bubbles?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Many economists call them that: prices far above what profits can justify. Home prices seem to have done the same in the 2000s, and their fall is where the 2008 crisis began. When those prices crash, people feel poorer and spend less.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in part one we saw three facts. Lenders asked much more for risk, the Fed's rate was stuck at zero for years, and share prices climbed far above profits before both great crashes.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Right. Next branch: a model that puts these facts together.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Part two of the map: Friction, deflation and the zero lower bound. The first leaf is an equation: the rate firms pay is the Fed's rate plus a risk premium. A jump in that premium works like a fall in demand.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: A financial friction makes borrowing more expensive. Here it's the risk premium. In calm times it is small and steady, so in practice the Fed sets the rate firms pay. In a panic, it jumps.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And why is that like a fall in demand?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Remember the IS curve. Firms compare the rate on a loan with the return on new capital, what a new machine or shed earns each year as a share of its cost. Take Harbor Boatworks, the island's boatyard. When the premium makes its loans cost more, it builds fewer boats, even if the central bank's rate hasn't changed. So spending and output fall, as if islanders had decided to spend less. To keep the rate firms pay the same, the central bank must cut one extra point for each point of premium.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: 2008. The Fed cuts to zero, but the premium jumps to 4 points, and output ends at minus 4 percent. How do we get there?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Let's build that number step by step, on Islandia. Here every rate is a real rate, after taking out inflation. We measure output as a percent gap from potential output, its normal level. It starts at zero. The return on new capital is 2 percent, and so is the Bank of Islandia's real rate. The premium is zero. Each point that firms pay above that return costs 1 percent of output.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then the housing bubble bursts.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Islanders feel poorer and spend less, so demand falls by 2 percent of potential output. With no response, output would be minus 2 percent.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But the Bank cuts its real rate from 2 percent to zero, 2 points below the return on capital. That adds back 2 points, and output is back at potential.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Right, the cut cancels the housing crash. Now the panic adds a premium of 4 points, about the jump we saw in the data.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: The Bank has already cut to zero, so I'd guess output stays at potential.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That's the tempting answer, but let's check. What do firms pay now?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Zero plus 4, so 4 percent.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That's 2 points above the return on capital. It costs 2 points of output, on top of the crash's 2. So output is minus 4 percent, twice as deep as the crash alone. Why doesn't the Bank cut further? Two leaves on, we meet the floor.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: the new AD curve, where inflation drifts to minus 4 percent. What's an AD curve again?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: AD means aggregate demand, total spending. The AD curve links inflation to output through the rule of Chapter 13. When inflation falls below the 2 percent target, the central bank cuts its real rate, one point for each point. This time the Bank follows that rule instead of cutting at once. So the 2-point crash and the 4-point premium make one sudden hit to demand, a shock, of 6 points.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then output falls by 6 percent?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Only by 4 percent in the first year. As output falls, the Phillips curve pulls inflation down, half a point for each point of the gap, and the rule cuts the rate. Things settle where both agree: output minus 4, inflation zero.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So inflation is 2 points below target, and the rule cuts the real rate by 2 points, to zero.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Exactly. That takes back 2 of the 6 points, so the rule softens the hit. After that, inflation keeps falling and the rule keeps cutting, and each year about one third of the remaining gap closes.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Where does it end?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Output is back at potential only when the rule has cut the rate by the full 6 points. By the rule, inflation is then 6 points below the 2 percent target: minus 4 percent. Prices falling year after year is called deflation.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Is that what happened after 2008?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Not quite. U.S. inflation stayed low but stopped falling, perhaps because people trusted the 2 percent target. And the model needs cuts below zero in money terms, which the next leaf shows is impossible.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: the zero lower bound. The real rate is the nominal rate minus inflation, and the nominal rate can't go below zero. What's a nominal rate?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: It's the rate in the news, in money terms, like the 0.19 percent of part one. It has a floor, a lowest level, near zero, because islanders can always hold cash, which earns zero. So at a zero nominal rate, the real rate is minus inflation.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in the 2008 leaf, did the floor stop our Bank at a real rate of zero?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: It depends on inflation. With inflation at zero, as in a deep slump, a zero nominal rate is a zero real rate. Then the Bank was already at the floor, and minus 4 was the best it could do.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And if inflation were still at its 2 percent target?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Then a zero nominal rate is a real rate of minus 2. Firms pay that plus the premium of 4, so 2 percent, just the return on capital. The rate does no harm, and only the crash's minus 2 is left.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But to close the gap, firms must pay zero, so the Bank needed a real rate of minus 4.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes, so a nominal rate of minus 2, below the floor. That's the answer to today's question in one line: the premium called for a cut below zero.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And if prices start to fall?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Then it gets worse. With prices falling 2 percent a year, a zero nominal rate is a real rate of plus 2, so firms pay 6 percent.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's 4 points above the return on capital.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: So it costs 4 points, on top of the crash's 2: output is minus 6.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last leaf of this part: the deflationary spiral of the Great Depression. Minus 3, minus 6, minus 9 percent. What are those numbers?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Output in three steps of our model. Before the crash, output is at potential and inflation is about zero. Step one: worried about a bubble in shares, the Fed raises its rate by 3 points. Output falls to minus 3 percent.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And step two is the crash of October 1929.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Yes. The crash cuts spending by another 3 points, so output is minus 6 percent. Step three is the dangerous one. The slump pulls inflation down by 3 points, from about zero to minus 3.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So prices are falling, and the Fed keeps its nominal rate where it was.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Exactly. So the real rate rises by 3 points, and output falls to minus 9 percent.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And then? I'd guess output recovers, as it did under the rule.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Here's the surprise: it's the opposite. Under the rule, falling inflation brought rate cuts. Now the nominal rate is frozen, so falling inflation raises the real rate. From there, inflation falls even faster, the real rate rises again, and output falls again. Each year's gap is one and a half times the last: minus 6 became minus 9, and next year is worse. That's the spiral. In the real Depression, prices fell by about a quarter from 1929 to 1933.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in part two we saw that the premium acts like a fall in demand. The zero floor blocks the cuts that would offset it, and falling prices can make the slump deeper and deeper.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Next branch: what policy did when its usual tool was stuck.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Part three of the map: Policy and the aftermath. The first leaf: money kept growing, as M1 growth went from 7 to 17 percent in late 2008. Why does that matter?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Because of the 1930s. M1 is cash, meaning notes and coins, plus the bank accounts people pay from. The economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed the Great Depression on a Fed that let the money supply fall from 1929 to 1933.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I'd guess money shrank again. Banks were scared and stopped lending.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Look at the data first: not this time. Between October and December 2008, the growth of M1 over the past year jumped from about 7 to about 17 percent. Growing money helps keep prices from falling, and part two showed why that matters.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: quantitative easing. By 2015, the Fed's assets, everything it owned, were worth five times as much as before. What did it buy?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Quantitative easing, or QE, means buying assets other than short-term government bonds, on a huge scale. The Fed bought long-term government bonds and bundles of home loans, to push down the long-term rates that firms and families pay.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the Fed printed trillions of dollars. High inflation must have followed.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That's a common belief, but it isn't what happened. The Fed paid mostly by adding to the deposits that banks keep at the Fed, called reserves. New cash paid for only about 15 percent. Cash gets spent in shops, but the Fed pays interest on reserves, so banks mostly held on to them. Inflation stayed low for more than a decade after QE began.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: forward guidance. The expected rate was cut to 0.57 percent in June 2012. Expected by whom?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: By financial markets. Forward guidance means telling markets how long the rate will stay low. A long-term rate is roughly the average of the short-term rates expected over the life of the loan. So a promise of low rates for longer lowers long-term rates today.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Can we put numbers on it?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Take a four-year loan. If markets expect short rates of zero, 1, 2 and 3 percent, the four-year rate is about their average, 1.5 percent.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And if the Fed promises zero for three years?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Then markets expect zero for three years, and 2 percent in the fourth. The average falls to one half of a percent.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And in 2012?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In January 2012, the Fed said its rate would likely stay very low until at least late 2014. Markets believed it: by June, they expected only 0.57 percent for the end of 2014.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next leaf: potential GDP revised down 10 percent, and productivity growing 0.72 percent a year since 2004. Let's start with potential GDP.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Potential GDP is the total output the economy would produce with its workers and machines in normal use. The Congressional Budget Office, or CBO, estimates it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: About ten years after the crisis, GDP was back at potential. So I'd guess the economy recovered everything it had lost.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That's what the gap says, but look at how it closed. In 2017, GDP was less than 1 percent below the CBO's latest estimate of potential.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And against the old estimate?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Almost 11 percent below the potential the CBO expected back in 2007. So the estimate itself came down by about 10 percent. The economy never got back to the output expected before the crisis.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Why was it lowered?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Low investment after the crisis, and slower productivity. Total factor productivity, or TFP, measures how well an economy uses its machines and workers. In private business, it grew more than 1.5 percent a year from 1995 to 2004.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And since 2004?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Only 0.72 percent a year, less than half as fast. But the slowdown began before the crisis, so the crisis can't be its only cause.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last leaf: policy, three topics: QE, fiscal stimulus and bubbles. What about fiscal stimulus?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Fiscal stimulus means the government buys more or cuts taxes. Normally, the central bank raises its rate when demand rises, which takes back part of the boost. At the floor, the rate stays at zero, so in our model each extra dollar of purchases adds a dollar of output. How much it adds in real life is still debated.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And bubbles. Should the central bank raise its rate to pop them?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: That's debated too. On one side, low Fed rates from 2002 to 2006 may have helped the housing boom grow. On the other, bubbles are hard to spot at the time, and a rate rise hits the whole economy. Many economists prefer a capital requirement instead. Capital here means the owners' own money in a bank, a cushion against losses. Islandia's banks keep a thin cushion, and the requirement makes it thicker.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: How does that help with bubbles?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: When a bubble bursts, the losses hit the owners' cushion first. So lenders worry less, and the premium jumps less.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So in part three we saw the Fed avoid the mistake of the 1930s and try new tools, while governments added spending. But output stayed below the old expectations, and productivity had already slowed.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Exactly. Let's sum up.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's go back to our three goals. First: why the premium hits like a fall in demand, and why a zero rate couldn't undo it.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Firms pay the central bank's rate plus the premium, so a higher premium cuts investment like a drop in demand. Offsetting it needed a nominal rate below zero. That's impossible, because people can always hold cash, which earns zero.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Second, the spiral.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: With the nominal rate stuck, falling prices raise the real rate. That deepens the slump, which makes prices fall faster, again and again.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And third, the other tools, and what came after.

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Money kept growing, the Fed bought long-term assets and promised low rates, and the government added spending. Still, output stayed below what was expected before the crisis. So here is the big message. A jump in the risk premium works like a collapse in demand, and the zero floor stops the central bank from offsetting it. Falling prices can then turn a recession into a spiral. So central banks and governments need tools beyond the interest rate.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's a question to think about. Suppose Islandia's central bank aimed for zero inflation instead of 2 percent. In the next crisis, how far below zero could it push the real rate, and why does that matter?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Pause the episode and think about it for a moment.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Okay, we're back. What's the answer?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: It couldn't push the real rate below zero at all. At a zero nominal rate, the real rate is minus inflation: minus 2 with 2 percent inflation, but only zero with zero inflation. On Islandia, the best output at the floor falls from minus 2 to minus 4 percent. That's one reason central banks aim for a little inflation, not zero.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Where can students try all this themselves?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: Open the chapter's Colab notebook to run every example yourself. The Model Apps let you move the premium without code, and the Data Apps show the charts.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And next time?

segments.speaker: ECONOMIST
segments.text: In Chapter 15, we meet DSGE models, the modern models of business cycles, the ups and downs of the economy. We ask: do productivity shocks cause recessions, and how do sticky wages and prices change the answer? Sticky means slow to change.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's it for today. Thanks for listening, and see you next time.
